title: Planarity dichotomy for induced subdivision detection
formal: Assuming \(\mathrm P\ne\mathrm{NP}\), is it true that for every fixed finite subcubic graph \(H\), detecting an induced subdivision of \(H\) in an arbitrary input graph belongs to \(\mathrm P\) if and only if \(H\) is planar?
why: A resolution would give one structural explanation for the complexity of an entire family of induced pattern-detection problems. It asks whether the geometry of the fixed pattern, rather than just its bounded degree, controls tractability.
status_note: The published 2025 paper explicitly states Conjecture 5 under P ≠ NP. The statement and model were checked on 13 September 2026; the bounded subsequent-work search supplied no verified resolution. Status is source_open.

progress.text: The paper proves hardness for a particular fixed subcubic induced-subdivision pattern and states the general planarity characterization as Conjecture 5.

sentences: For a fixed graph H, induced-subdivision detection asks whether an input graph contains a subdivided copy of H as an induced subgraph.
Extra edges between selected vertices are forbidden.
The conjecture concerns patterns H of maximum degree three and predicts tractability exactly for planar patterns, assuming P differs from NP.
Existing algorithms and hardness constructions motivate the proposed boundary.
This would classify a natural family of pattern-detection problems by a geometric property of the fixed pattern itself.

definitions: All graphs are finite, undirected and simple. Subcubic means maximum degree at most three; \(H\) need not be connected. A subdivision of \(H\) is obtained by replacing each edge by a path of positive length, with pairwise disjoint internal vertex sets, none of which contains a vertex of \(H\). An induced subdivision in \(G\) is a set \(W\subseteq V(G)\) such that the induced graph \(G[W]\) is isomorphic to a subdivision of \(H\). Equivalently, choose distinct branch vertices for all vertices of \(H\), including its isolated vertices, and replacement paths with exactly the prescribed edges and no additional edges anywhere among the selected vertices. For each fixed \(H\), the decision problem takes only \(G\), encoded by its binary adjacency matrix, and answers whether such \(W\) exists; no degree, planarity or connectivity promise is made on \(G\). Polynomial time means a deterministic Turing machine with running time \(C_H(|V(G)|+1)^{k_H}\) for constants depending on \(H\), but not on \(G\). An algorithm need not be uniform in the pattern \(H\), which is not part of the input. Planarity means admitting a crossing-free drawing in the plane. The complexity assumption uses the ordinary uniform deterministic and nondeterministic polynomial-time language classes.

context_blocks.text: The source proposes planarity of a fixed subcubic pattern as the complete boundary for tractable induced-subdivision detection. Its assumption P ≠ NP is essential to the stated if-and-only-if claim.

The paper exhibits a fixed subcubic pattern whose induced-subdivision containment problem is NP-complete. This establishes an obstruction within low-degree patterns but does not classify every such pattern. Induced containment additionally forbids unwanted edges between the selected paths, unlike ordinary subdivision containment.

answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the universal equivalence under the stated P ≠ NP hypothesis, or a proof of its negation under that hypothesis. A counterexample must identify a fixed subcubic pattern and establish the failure of the corresponding direction. Proving hardness for one nonplanar pattern, or algorithms for only some planar patterns, does not settle the whole conjecture. NP-completeness of every nonplanar case would suffice for that direction but is not silently added as a stronger required conclusion.

notes: Restored the omitted P ≠ NP hypothesis rather than asserting the source equivalence unconditionally.
Defined induced subdivisions including isolated pattern vertices, internal disjointness and all forbidden extra edges; distinguished fixed-pattern complexity from an algorithm uniform in H.
Preserved the source in-P iff planar claim instead of silently strengthening all nonplanar cases to NP-completeness.
